newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. council reprimands Libya on violating air ban.
newsitem.headline: U.N. council reprimands Libya on violating air ban.

text.p: The Security Council reprimanded Libya on Wednesday for saying it no longer considered itself subject to a mandatory U.N. air embargo and called a recent flight to Ghana by a Libyan plane "an apparent violation" of sanctions.
A statement read at a brief public meeting by council President Hisashi Owada of Japan said the committee that oversees sanctions against Libya had been asked to "follow up this matter."

The Security Council imposed mandatory sanctions on Libya in 1992, including a ban on all international flights, for failing to extradite two men wanted by Britain and the United States for the 1988 mid-air bombing of a Pan Am airliner over Lockerbie, Scotland, which killed 270 people.

The council's statement was in reaction to a recent letter from Libya saying that since it gave permission, at U.S. insistence, for an American-piloted balloon to overfly its territory earlier this month, it would henceforth allow all aircraft to land at Libyan airports and would resume flights abroad by Libyan Arab Airways.
A Libyan plane then flew an official delegation to Accra, Ghana, and returned to Tripoli.
The council said it noted the Libyan letter "with concern" and considered it to be "incompatible" with the 1992 sanctions resolution.

It said the sanctions did not prohibit overflights of Libyan territory -- rejecting Libya's claim that allowing balloonist Steve Fossett to pass over Libya in the course of an unsuccessful round-the-world attempt meant the sanctions no longer applied.
The sanctions did, however, "prohibit all international flights to and from Libya" and the council would "consider any such flights to be a violation," the statement said.

Taking note of "the reports that a Libyan-registered aircraft, in apparent violation" of the sanctions, flew from Tripoli to Accra on January 21 and later departed, the council said it had asked its sanctions committee to "follow up this matter."

A council source said China and Egypt had tried to prevent inclusion in the statement of any reference to a violation of sanctions. The source also said the fact the statement was issued at a formal council meeting, instead of just being read to reporters as sometimes happens, indicated a stiffening of the council's attitude.

Libya has violated sanctions on several previous occasions. It flew Moslem pilgrims to and from Saudi Arabia in 1995 and 1996, and last June it flew Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi to Cairo and back to attend an Arab summit meeting.
The council statement also drew the attention of U.N. members to their obligations under the sanctions "in the event that Libyan-registered aircraft seek to land in their territory."
All countries are required to bar any planes flying to or from Libya from landing in, taking off from, or overflying their territory.
